result: The study used EAAT4-GFP transgenic mice to target specific cerebellar modules defined by zebrin II expression patterns. Viral tracing of mossy fiber projections from the external cuneate nucleus and spinal cord revealed mutually exclusive parasagittal bands in lobules III/IV, with 22% of cuneate projections found contralaterally. The combination of climbing fiber and mossy fiber inputs delimited 13 regions with unique input combinations between P2+ bands.
evaluation: Claims C2, C38-C44, and C112 collectively establish the experimental approach and anatomical characterization. The use of EAAT4-GFP mice is validated by immunohistochemistry (C112), viral tracing provides quantitative data on projection patterns (C40-C41), and the identification of 13 distinct regions is supported by anatomical mapping (C44). The methodology is well-documented with appropriate controls.

result: Photostimulation mapping revealed highly heterogeneous patterns of granule cell inputs to Purkinje cells, with 38% of sites being silent, dense local inputs (mean 10.3±13.8 pC), and remotely connected patches at distances averaging 215±86 μm. In 5 of 49 cells, no obvious local inputs were observed despite the presence of distal inputs, demonstrating that distant granule cells can make strong connections via parallel fibers.
evaluation: Claims C3, C46-C52 present the core experimental findings from photostimulation experiments with quantitative data (n=49 cells). The methodology is validated by control experiments (C113-C119) showing appropriate stimulation parameters and ruling out technical artifacts. The heterogeneous connectivity patterns are well-documented with specific percentages and measurements.

result: Neighboring Purkinje cells belonging to the same microzone displayed similar granule cell synaptic input maps, with significant correlation found in 8 of 9 pairs of adjacent recorded PCs (r=0.74±0.14). This suggests that neighboring PCs make powerful connections with specific sets of distant microzones while ignoring others.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by paired recording experiments with quantitative correlation analysis. The finding that 8/9 pairs showed significant correlation (C53) provides strong evidence for shared connectivity rules among neighboring PCs (C54-C55). The statistical analysis is appropriate for the data.

result: Correlation matrix analysis revealed four clusters of PC groups displaying highly correlated GC connectivity maps that are stereotyped and consistent across animals (N=49 PCs from 18 animals). These functional clusters do not strictly match anatomical boundaries defined by zebrin II bands or mossy fiber inputs, though all PC groups showed strong connections in ipsilateral P2+ and silent regions in P1−.
evaluation: Claims C56-C62, C85, and C88 describe the computational analysis identifying stereotyped patterns. The use of spectral co-clustering (C56) and correlation analysis across multiple animals provides robust evidence for consistent functional organization. The mismatch with anatomical boundaries (C58-C59) is a key finding supported by direct comparison with zebrin and MF input patterns.

result: The functional synaptic organization of granule cell inputs to Purkinje cells, molecular layer interneurons, and Golgi cells displays position-specific patterns that connect distant cortical modules but do not strictly match with anatomical boundaries defined by zebrin bands or mossy fiber inputs from the spinocerebellar or cuneate pathways.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C58-C59, C90, and C101 collectively establish that functional connectivity patterns differ from anatomical organization. This is supported by direct comparison of functional maps with anatomical markers across multiple cell types. The finding is consistent across different experimental approaches (photostimulation mapping, anatomical tracing).

result: Granule cell inputs to Golgi cells were predominantly local, with 81% of synaptic inputs made by local GCs within a mean extension of 114.1±70.1 μm, matching the range of the GoC axonal plexus (214±30 μm). This connectivity pattern was not limited by zebrin boundaries and appears restricted to intra-microzonal communication, implementing a local inhibitory feedback circuit.
evaluation: Claims C64-C67 and C87 are supported by quantitative data from 19 GoC recordings with anatomical reconstructions. The local restriction of GC-GoC connectivity contrasts with the long-range GC-PC connectivity, providing evidence for cell-type-specific connectivity rules. Control experiments with carbenoxolone ruled out gap junction artifacts.

result: Granule cell connectivity patterns to molecular layer interneurons showed both local and distant hotspots that did not perfectly overlap with GC inputs to PCs in the same area, indicating that different groups of GC inputs can be selected for PCs and MLIs. This suggests GCs relay mossy fiber information through two distinct pathways: MF-GC-PC and MF-GC-MLI-PC, enabling long-distance communication between microzones.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 and C86 are supported by comparative analysis of GC connectivity to different cell types (n=7 MLIs). The differential connectivity patterns between PCs and MLIs in the same region (C68-C69) provide evidence for parallel processing pathways (C70, C86). The data support cell-type-specific connectivity rules.

result: Activity-dependent plasticity can modify granule cell connectivity maps. A 1 Hz stimulation protocol induced LTP or LTD at 22% of sites (86/~390 sites, n=8 cells), with stronger connections undergoing LTD and weaker connections undergoing LTP. Of 56 potentiated sites, 33 were initially silent, demonstrating that previously undetectable synaptic connections can be awakened. Silent sites at any mediolateral position could be specifically awakened by targeted stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C6, C71-C84, C94-C95 describe plasticity experiments with appropriate controls (C73) and quantitative measurements. The bidirectional plasticity (LTP/LTD) is supported by cited literature and pharmacological controls. The awakening of silent synapses (C76-C77, C82-C83) is demonstrated by targeted stimulation experiments. The negative correlation between initial synaptic weight and plasticity direction (C74-C75) provides mechanistic insight.

result: Connectivity patterns were found to be consistent and predictable between animals, suggesting that specific sets of cerebellar functional microzones are reproducibly combined together following similar operational rules.
evaluation: Claims C7, C88-C89 are supported by the correlation analysis across 18 animals showing stereotyped patterns. The identification of four consistent PC clusters (C56-C57) across animals provides strong evidence for reproducible functional organization. However, the claim about 'operational rules' (C89) is somewhat inferential.

result: Granule cell patches likely combine mossy fiber information from different sources, and functional microzones likely compute information from different sources of MF inputs, frequently belonging to two adjacent zebrin bands.
evaluation: Claims C102 and C105 are inferences supported by the mismatch between functional connectivity patterns and single MF input sources (C101). The claims are supported by citations to recent studies and are consistent with the observation that functional clusters span zebrin boundaries. However, direct demonstration of multi-source integration would strengthen these claims.

result: The stereotyped organization of GC inputs suggests that microzones may have specific roles in behavioral tasks associated with the anterior vermis, such as adaptive locomotion. The area between P2+ ipsi- and contralateral bands could be composed of 10-13 functional units with mean extension of 70-100 μm, which might combine multiple biochemical toolboxes for information processing.
evaluation: Claims C91, C104, C106-C107 are largely speculative about functional implications, supported by citations but not directly tested in this study. While the anatomical and connectivity data are solid, the behavioral relevance (C91, C104) and the specific number of functional units (C107) require additional experimental validation. These represent reasonable hypotheses based on the data but are not directly demonstrated.

result: The mechanisms underlying bidirectional plasticity involve calcium-dependent processes, with focal PF stimulation likely evoking large calcium transients leading to LTD at the center of the beam, while sparse peripheral activation induces moderate transients leading to LTP. LTP could favor information transfer between microzones, while LTD could limit such communication.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 are mechanistic speculations supported by citations but not directly tested with calcium imaging or other mechanistic experiments in this study. While the proposed mechanisms are consistent with established literature (Hartell 1996, Coesmans et al. 2004), they remain hypothetical in the context of the observed plasticity patterns. The functional roles of LTP and LTD (C99-C100) are reasonable inferences but lack direct experimental support.

result: Discrepancies with previous in vivo studies showing predominantly local GC inputs to PCs might be explained by regional differences in cerebellar operational rules or by methodological limitations of using PC firing rate modulation to define receptive fields, which could mask correlated excitatory and inhibitory input changes.
evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are speculative explanations for discrepancies with prior literature. While these are reasonable hypotheses, they are not directly tested in this study. The regional specificity hypothesis (C92) would require systematic comparison across cerebellar regions, and the methodological critique (C93) would require simultaneous measurement of excitation and inhibition in vivo.

result: Communication between microzones through parallel fibers is proposed as a general mechanism in cerebellar information processing that favors PC synchronization within specific modules and improves information readout by nuclear cells. This mechanism may extend beyond the anterior vermis to other cerebellar regions including the posterior lobe.
evaluation: Claims C103, C108-C111 involve generalizations beyond the experimental data. While C103 is supported by citation, the generality of the mechanism (C109) and its functional consequences (C111) are speculative. The study focused on lobules III/IV of the anterior vermis, so extension to other regions (C108) requires additional experimental validation. These represent reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support in this manuscript.

result: Control experiments measuring granule cell layer slope showed mean deviation of 0.85±0.82 degrees from horizontal (130 axons, 13 slices), ruling out slice tilt as an explanation for the absence of distal responses in some cases.
evaluation: Claims C118-C119 describe important control experiments that validate the experimental approach. The quantitative measurement of slice orientation (C118) and the inference that tilt does not explain the results (C119) are well-supported by the data. This addresses a potential technical artifact.
